title: You haven't been there (Avot 2:4)
hook: Hillel: don't separate from the community; don't judge until you've stood in their place

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rabban Gamaliel's mirror, ratzon: do God's will as your own. Your line was want what's good. Did you find a reason to want it? Today, Hillel is back. Day two hundred fifty-three.

The woman in the checkout line snaps at her kid, and everyone around her silently decides what kind of mother she is. The coworker who's been late three times this month. The neighbor who never mows his lawn. These verdicts arrive in an instant, and they feel very sure. What we don't see is the hospital visit that morning, or the second job, or the thing nobody talks about at home. Hillel, the gentle sage from the roof in the snow, has five short warnings in chapter two. The middle one is about exactly this.
screen: `THE MOTHER IN THE CHECKOUT LINE.` → `AN INSTANT, VERY SURE.` → `WHAT WE DON'T SEE.`

segments.voice: Here are Hillel's warnings. Don't separate yourself from the community. Don't be sure of yourself until the day you die. Don't judge your fellow until you've reached his place. Don't say something that can't be understood, hoping it'll be understood later. And don't say, when I have free time I'll study, because maybe you won't. Look at the middle one. Don't judge your fellow until you've reached his place. Makom in Hebrew: his place, his spot, where he's standing. Not until you've heard about it. Until you've gotten there. Now look at the line right before it: don't be sure of yourself until the day you die. The Talmud tells of a high priest who served faithfully for eighty years, and then, at the very end, left the path of the sages. Nobody is beyond slipping. Put those two lines side by side and you see what Hillel is doing. You can't be too sure about yourself, and you can't be too sure about the other person. You don't know how you'd act in their place, because you've never stood there. Some teachers point out something quietly radical in the wording. Can you ever really reach another person's place? Their childhood, their body, their worst morning? Maybe never completely. Which would mean the judgment always waits. That doesn't mean anything goes. Jewish law has courts and judges. But in everyday life, Hillel asks for a pause, and a little humility, before the verdict.
screen: `HILLEL'S FIVE WARNINGS.` · `UNTIL YOU'VE REACHED HIS PLACE.` · `DON'T BE SURE OF YOURSELF.` · `CAN YOU EVER REACH IT?` · then, large: `YOU HAVEN'T BEEN THERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: stand in someone's place. Settle, and breathe. Think of one person you've judged lately. Don't argue about whether you were right. Just imagine waking up in their bed this morning. Their worries. Their body. Their bank account. The conversation they're dreading. Walk through their morning slowly, until they get to the moment you judged. Notice if anything shifts. The bell holds the time.
Makom. His place, where he stands: the word in Hillel's warning not to judge your fellow until you've reached it.
Your line: nobody is beyond slipping. Today, when a quick judgment rises, hold it back once, and wonder what their morning was like. Day two hundred fifty-three.

howItsDone: Hillel's warning is studied alongside the teaching to judge every person favorably, as a daily habit of thought.

fork.setup: a coworker has been late three times this month, and the whole office is talking. what does Hillel say?
options: hold the judgment. you haven't been in their place.
fork.reveal: don't judge your fellow until you've reached his place, Hillel says, and don't be too sure of yourself either.

original.note: Mishnaic Hebrew: until you reach his place.

trapdoor: what you thought: don't be judgmental.
what it means: you can't be sure of them, and you can't be sure of yourself, so pause before the verdict.
what a scholar hears: some teachers note you can never fully reach another's place, so in daily life the judgment always waits.

notes: The high priest who served 80 years and became a Sadducee is Yochanan the High Priest, Berakhot 29a; the script says 'left the path of the sages' rather than naming the Sadducees; confirm.
'You can never fully reach another's place, so the judgment always waits' is a reading found among later teachers (sometimes attributed to Hasidic or Musar sources); confirm or attribute.
Five warnings of Hillel in 2:4 (some editions split 2:4–2:5); confirm.
